rubric_v1_gloss: “To delight in talking about other men's failings is called calumny.”

teaching.quote: … To delight in talking about other men’s failings is called calumny. …
teaching.citation: Zhuangzi 31 The Old Fisherman, trans. Burton Watson 2013, stranger speaking

limits: The marker is delight, not falsehood. Watson’s “calumny” should not be read as requiring slander.

rubric_v1_gloss: “To speak without regard for what is right or wrong is called flattery.”

teaching.quote: … To speak without regard for what is right or wrong is called flattery. …
teaching.citation: Zhuangzi 31 The Old Fisherman, trans. Burton Watson 2013, stranger speaking

limits: The fault is speech unmoored from right and wrong, not praise as such. It overlaps with treachery’s “without thought for right or wrong.”

rubric_v1_gloss: “To break up friendships and set kinfolk at odds is called maliciousness.”

teaching.quote: … To break up friendships and set kinfolk at odds is called maliciousness. … These eight faults inflict chaos on others and injury on the possessor.
teaching.citation: Zhuangzi 31 The Old Fisherman, trans. Burton Watson 2013, stranger speaking

limits: The fault requires an agent who divides people. The source gives no motive requirement and no exceptions.

rubric_v1_gloss: “To rush forward when no one has nodded in your direction is called obsequiousness.”
source_scope: Zhuangzi 31 eight faults (Watson tr.): the stranger’s definition, spoken to Confucius.

teaching.quote: … To rush forward when no one has nodded in your direction is called obsequiousness. … These eight faults inflict chaos on others and injury on the possessor.
teaching.citation: Zhuangzi 31 The Old Fisherman, trans. Burton Watson 2013, stranger speaking

limits: The source gives only a one-sentence definition, and gives no reason for the nod requirement. Ordinary deference is not resistance.

rubric_v1_gloss: “To do what it is not your business to do is called officiousness.”
source_scope: The fisherman’s lesson to Confucius in Zhuangzi 31 (Watson tr., disputed chapter): eight faults, with role context.

teaching.quote: “Moreover, there are eight faults that men may possess … To do what it is not your business to do is called officiousness. … These eight faults inflict chaos on others and injury on the possessor.
teaching.citation: Zhuangzi 31 The Old Fisherman, trans. Burton Watson 2013, stranger speaking

teaching.quote: When officials attend to their duties and men worry about their undertakings, there is no overstepping of the mark. … Now on the higher level, you do not hold the position of a ruler, a feudal lord, or a chancellor, and on the lower level, you have not been assigned to the office of a high minister with its tasks and duties. Yet you presume to ‘bring a beautiful order to rites and music, … ’ This is undertaking rather a lot, isn’t it?
teaching.citation: Zhuangzi 31 The Old Fisherman, trans. Burton Watson 2013, stranger speaking

limits: The fault turns on business that is not one’s own. Helping when one is asked, or acting within one’s role, is not evidence of it.

rubric_v1_gloss: “To echo a man's opinions and try to draw him out in speech is called sycophancy.”
source_scope: Zhuangzi 31 eight faults (Watson tr.): a fault of speech and service.

teaching.quote: … To echo a man’s opinions and try to draw him out in speech is called sycophancy. …
teaching.citation: Zhuangzi 31 The Old Fisherman, trans. Burton Watson 2013, stranger speaking

limits: Agreement alone is not this fault. The source does not explain why the echoer draws the other out.

rubric_v1_gloss: “Without thought for right or wrong, to try to face in two directions at once so as to steal a glimpse of the other party's wishes is called treachery.”
source_scope: Zhuangzi 31 eight faults (Watson tr.): two-faced probing, not every betrayal.

teaching.quote: … Without thought for right or wrong, to try to face in two directions at once so as to steal a glimpse of the other party’s wishes is called treachery. These eight faults inflict chaos on others and injury on the possessor.
teaching.citation: Zhuangzi 31 The Old Fisherman, trans. Burton Watson 2013, stranger speaking

limits: Watson’s “treachery” is technical. It overlaps with flattery’s disregard of right and wrong.

rubric_v1_gloss: “To praise falsely and hypocritically so as to cause injury and evil to others is called wickedness.”
source_scope: Zhuangzi 31 eight faults (Watson tr.): a defined term, not any immoral act.

teaching.quote: … To praise falsely and hypocritically so as to cause injury and evil to others is called wickedness. …
teaching.citation: Zhuangzi 31 The Old Fisherman, trans. Burton Watson 2013, stranger speaking

limits: The term is narrow, unlike generic English “wickedness.” Harm done without false praise belongs elsewhere.
